_about: Drafted reasons for predictor failures, one per FAMILY, plus per-pair overrides keyed stat|A|B (either order; the 32 Phase 1 drafts).
DRAFTS from Claude's training knowledge, NOT verified against a source. A family marked confidence: lower is the one to read most carefully.
The teacher reviews a family's reason (and any overrides in it) and runs: python tools/review_family.py <family>
Every computed upset must be listed in exactly one family, or the build fails. Regenerate exceptions.json with: node tools/build_exceptions.mjs

radius-high-spin-average.label: Mn and Fe radii average two spin states
radius-high-spin-average.reason: The dataset gives manganese and iron the average of a low-spin and a high-spin covalent radius, and high-spin atoms are much larger, so the averaged values come out above chromium's instead of below it.

radius-3d-upturn.label: Radii turn up at the end of the 3d row
radius-3d-upturn.reason: Near the end of the 3d row radii stop shrinking and grow again: once the 3d subshell is nearly full, the added d electrons repel one another and screen the extra protons, so copper comes out larger than nickel.

radius-flat-late-p-block.label: Flat radii late in periods 4-6
radius-flat-late-p-block.reason: Late in periods 4 to 6 the across-period shrink almost disappears, because filled d (and f) shells underneath shield the added protons poorly; these radii differ by only 1 to 2 pm, close to the dataset's own uncertainty.

radius-astatine-estimate.label: Astatine's radius is an estimate
radius-astatine-estimate.reason: Astatine's radius rests on very few measured structures, and in the nearly flat period-6 p-block a small error in that estimate is enough to flip the order.

ie-s-to-p-drop.label: s-to-p drop
ie-s-to-p-drop.reason: The element with the lower value is removing a single p electron that sits just above a filled s subshell. A p electron is higher in energy and better shielded than an s electron, so it comes off more easily even though the trend says it should be harder.

ie-half-filled-p.label: Half-filled p subshell
ie-half-filled-p.reason: The element further right has to pair a p electron in an orbital that is already occupied, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove than an electron from the half-filled p subshell next door.

ie-poor-d-f-shielding.label: Poor shielding by filled d and f shells
ie-poor-d-f-shielding.reason: The heavier element's outer electrons sit outside filled d (and in period 6, f) shells that shield the nucleus poorly, so the extra protons pull harder than expected and the usual drop down the group disappears.

ie-6p-spin-orbit.label: The 6p level splits
ie-6p-spin-orbit.reason: In period 6 the 6p level splits in two; bismuth's third 6p electron goes into the higher level and comes off more easily than one of lead's two lower-level electrons.

ie-zinc-filled-subshells.label: Zinc's filled subshells
ie-zinc-filled-subshells.reason: Zinc's outer 4s pair sits outside a complete 3d subshell and feels the nuclear charge built up across the whole d-block, so zinc has the highest first ionization energy of the 3d row, higher even than lighter p-block elements the trend expects to beat it.

ie-3d-metal-4s-vs-p.label: A 3d metal's 4s electron vs a p electron
ie-3d-metal-4s-vs-p.reason: A 3d metal loses a 4s electron, which penetrates close to the nucleus and feels the nuclear charge that builds across the d-block. The p-block element's outer p electron sits higher in energy and is better shielded, so it comes off more easily, against the trend.

ie-3d-row-flat.label: Nearly flat ionization energies across the 3d row
ie-3d-row-flat.reason: Across the 3d row the electron removed is a 4s electron, and each added proton arrives with an added 3d electron that partly shields it, so first ionization energies barely change; small shifts in how the 3d electrons are arranged decide the order instead of the trend.

en-poor-d-f-shielding.label: Poor shielding by filled d and f shells
en-poor-d-f-shielding.reason: The heavier element's valence electrons sit outside filled d (and in period 6, f) shells that shield the nucleus poorly, so it pulls on bonding electrons about as hard as the lighter element or harder, instead of less.

en-xenon.label: Xenon's value comes from few compounds
en-xenon.reason: Xenon's Pauling value comes from its few compounds with fluorine and oxygen, and a noble gas does not continue the across-period rise, so iodine comes out higher.

en-3d-vs-light-p.label: 3d metals outpull aluminum and silicon
en-3d-vs-light-p.reason: Most 3d metals have Pauling values a little above aluminum's (and nickel's is just above silicon's): their bonding electrons feel nuclear charge that the 3d electrons screen poorly, so the drop expected from period 3 to period 4 does not happen.

en-mn-half-filled.label: Manganese's half-filled 3d subshell
en-mn-half-filled.reason: Manganese (3d5 4s2) has a half-filled 3d subshell, a stable arrangement that holds on to its own electrons, and its Pauling value dips below vanadium's and chromium's.

en-late-3d-peak.label: Electronegativity peaks at Ni-Cu, dips at Zn
en-late-3d-peak.reason: The across-period rule treats the 3d row and the p-block as one line, but Pauling electronegativity peaks around nickel and copper, drops at zinc, whose full 3d subshell takes no part in bonding, and climbs again through the p-block starting from gallium.

mass-isotope-mix.label: Isotope mix
mass-isotope-mix.reason: Atomic mass is an average over an element's natural isotopes. Here the element with fewer protons has more neutrons in its common isotopes, so it outweighs the next element even though atomic number says it should be lighter.

ea-period-2-crowding.label: Small period-2 atoms are crowded
ea-period-2-crowding.reason: The period-2 atom is so small that an added electron is crowded in with the electrons already there; that repulsion offsets the stronger pull of the nucleus, so the heavier atom in the same group releases more energy.

ea-group-13-vs-alkali.label: Group 13 holds an added p electron weakly
ea-group-13-vs-alkali.reason: A group 13 atom's added electron goes into a p orbital shielded by the filled s pair beneath it, so it is held weakly, while an alkali metal's added electron completes its s pair. The alkali metal releases slightly more energy, against the across-period rule.

ea-group-2-filled-s.label: Group 2's s subshell is already full
ea-group-2-filled-s.reason: A group 2 atom's s subshell is already full, so an added electron must go into a higher-energy orbital and almost no energy is released; an alkali metal's added electron completes its s pair and releases more.

ea-group-2-down.label: Group 2's tiny values rise down the group
ea-group-2-down.reason: Group 2 electron affinities are all tiny, because the added electron must sit outside a full s subshell. At such small values the down-a-group rule no longer holds: in larger atoms the empty orbitals lie closer in energy to the filled ones, so the heavier atoms take the electron a little more readily.

ea-3d-irregular.label: Irregular electron affinities in the 3d row
ea-3d-irregular.reason: Across the 3d row electron affinity jumps around instead of climbing: the added electron can enter a 3d or a 4s orbital, which are close in energy, so how much energy is released depends on the arrangement it makes. Scandium, titanium and iron release very little, less than the alkali metals (and, for titanium, barium) or their 3d neighbours.

ea-3d-beats-p.label: Some 3d metals beat nearby p-block elements
ea-3d-beats-p.reason: Several 3d metals release more energy on gaining an electron than nearby p-block elements. Copper's added electron completes its 4s pair (3d10 4s2) and nickel's nearly fills its 3d subshell, so both outscore the group 13 elements and even phosphorus, arsenic and germanium; vanadium, chromium and cobalt also outscore the group 13 elements, whose added p electron is weakly held.

ea-group-15-half-filled.label: Group 15's half-filled p subshell
ea-group-15-half-filled.reason: Group 15 atoms have a half-filled p subshell, so an added electron must pair up in an occupied orbital, which costs repulsion energy. That keeps their electron affinities below group 14's, and because the pairing cost is smaller in larger atoms, the values rise rather than fall going down the group.

ea-period-6-6p.label: The 6p level splits (thallium and lead)
ea-period-6-6p.reason: In period 6 the 6p level splits in two. Thallium's added electron fills the lower 6p level and is held well, so thallium beats indium; lead's lower 6p level is already full, so its added electron must go into the higher level and lead falls below thallium and cesium.

ionic-big-cation-small-anion.label: A large cation beats a small anion
ionic-big-cation-small-anion.reason: Anions are usually larger than cations, but this cation has more filled electron shells than the anion: K+, Rb+, Cs+ and Ba2+ keep three to five shells, while F- and O2- have only two, so the cation is the larger ion.

ionic-charge-differs.label: The charges differ
ionic-charge-differs.reason: These ions carry different charges, and the trend ignores that. The ion with the smaller positive charge has lost fewer electrons, so the nucleus holds the rest less tightly and the ion is larger, even though its element sits further right.

ionic-lone-pair.label: The ion keeps its outer s pair
ionic-lone-pair.reason: The ion further right keeps its outer s electron pair (Sb3+ keeps 5s2; Pb2+ and Bi3+ keep 6s2), while Sn4+ and Tl3+ have lost their whole outer shell, so the ion that keeps the pair is much larger.

ionic-same-charge-3d.label: Same charge, different 3d arrangement
ionic-same-charge-3d.reason: These ions have the same charge, yet the one further right is larger: in a six-coordinate site the arrangement of the 3d electrons changes the radius. High-spin Fe3+ (3d5) and the filled-shell ions Ga3+ and Zn2+ (3d10) put electrons in orbitals that point at their neighbours, and Cu2+ sits in a stretched site, so each comes out larger than the ion it is compared with.

overrides.radius_pm|As|Se: The Cordero radii of As (119 pm) and Se (120 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's own uncertainty: by group 15-16 of period 4 the across-period contraction has flattened because the filled 3d shell shields the added nuclear charge poorly.
overrides.radius_pm|As|Br: As (119 pm) and Br (120 pm) are 1 pm apart, within the Cordero uncertainty: the period-4 p-block radii level off after the 3d shell fills, so the across-period shrink is essentially gone by bromine.
overrides.radius_pm|Te|I: Te (138 pm) and I (139 pm) differ by 1 pm, inside the dataset's uncertainty: the across-period contraction has flattened by the end of period 5 as the 4d shell shields poorly and the bonds measured are to larger partners.
overrides.radius_pm|Tl|Pb: Tl (145 pm) and Pb (146 pm) are 1 pm apart: in the period-6 p-block the across-period shrink is cancelled by the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding, leaving the radii nearly flat.
overrides.radius_pm|Tl|Bi: Period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat (Tl 145, Pb 146, Bi 148 pm) because relativistic 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding offset the usual across-period decrease, and Bi's three 6p electrons sit in the slightly larger 6p3/2 level.
overrides.radius_pm|Tl|At: Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) is an estimate from very few structures, and the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat anyway, so the across-period shrink from Tl (145 pm) does not show in this dataset.
overrides.radius_pm|Pb|Bi: Pb (146 pm) and Bi (148 pm) are 2 pm apart in a period whose p-block radii barely change: the inert-pair 6s contraction and poor 4f/5d shielding cancel the usual across-period decrease.
overrides.radius_pm|Pb|At: Astatine's Cordero radius (150 pm) rests on very few structures and comes out larger than lead's (146 pm); the period-6 p-block radii are nearly flat, so a small data artifact is enough to flip the order.
overrides.radius_pm|Bi|At: Astatine's 150 pm Cordero value is an estimate from scarce structural data and exceeds bismuth's 148 pm; across the flat period-6 p-block that 2 pm difference is within the method's uncertainty.
overrides.radius_pm|Po|At: Polonium's Cordero radius (140 pm) comes from few structures and astatine's (150 pm) from fewer still; the 10 pm jump is a data artifact of a sparsely measured corner of the table, not a trend.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Be|B: Boron's outermost electron is in 2p, higher in energy and better shielded than beryllium's paired 2s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|N|O: Oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair up in an already occupied orbital, and that pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of nitrogen's three unpaired, half-filled 2p electrons.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Mg|Al: Aluminum's outermost electron is in 3p, higher in energy and better shielded than magnesium's paired 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove despite the extra proton.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Al|Ca: Aluminum's single 3p electron is unusually easy to remove (the s-to-p drop), while calcium is removing one of a filled 4s pair, so the heavier element edges ahead.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Al|Ga: Gallium's 4p electron sits outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so the extra nuclear charge pulls it slightly harder than expected and the usual drop down the group vanishes.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Al|Tl: Thallium's 6p electron is held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so its ionization energy is higher than aluminum's.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|P|S: Sulfur's fourth 3p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it easier to remove than one of phosphorus's three unpaired, half-filled 3p electrons.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Ca|Ga: Gallium's single 4p electron is higher in energy than calcium's paired 4s electrons, so even with eleven more protons gallium's first ionization energy comes out lower.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Ga|Tl: Thallium's 6p electron feels a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, and relativistic effects contract the inner shells further, so it is held more tightly than gallium's 4p electron.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|As|Se: Selenium's fourth 4p electron must pair up, and the pairing repulsion makes it slightly easier to remove than one of arsenic's three unpaired 4p electrons.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|In|Tl: The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's 6p electron poorly (the lanthanide contraction), so the nucleus holds it tighter than indium holds its 5p electron.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Sn|Pb: Lead's 6p electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so lead's ionization energy edges above tin's.
overrides.ie1_kjmol|Pb|Bi: In period 6 the 6p level splits strongly by spin-orbit coupling; bismuth's third 6p electron goes into the higher 6p3/2 level and is easier to remove than one of lead's lower 6p1/2 pair.
overrides.en_pauling|Al|Ga: Gallium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so gallium pulls bonding electrons harder than aluminum (the d-block contraction).
overrides.en_pauling|Al|In: Indium's valence electrons sit outside a filled 4d shell that shields poorly, so its electronegativity stays above aluminum's instead of falling down the group.
overrides.en_pauling|Al|Tl: Thallium's valence electrons are held by a nucleus poorly shielded by the 4f and 5d shells, with relativistic contraction adding to the pull, so it is more electronegative than aluminum.
overrides.en_pauling|Si|Ge: Germanium's 4p electrons sit outside a filled 3d shell that shields the nucleus poorly, so germanium pulls bonding electrons slightly harder than silicon (the d-block contraction).
overrides.en_pauling|Si|Sn: Tin's valence electrons sit outside filled 3d and 4d shells that shield poorly, so its electronegativity stays just above silicon's instead of falling down the group.
overrides.en_pauling|In|Tl: The 4f and 5d shells shield thallium's valence electrons poorly and relativistic contraction tightens its hold, so thallium is slightly more electronegative than indium.
overrides.en_pauling|I|Xe: Xenon's Pauling value (2.6) is derived from its few compounds with fluorine and oxygen, and a noble gas does not continue the across-period rise, so iodine comes out higher.
overrides.mass|Ar|K: Argon's dominant isotope is Ar-40 while potassium's is K-39, so argon averages heavier even with one fewer proton; Earth's Ar-40 is abundant because it is the decay product of K-40.
overrides.mass|Te|I: Tellurium's most abundant isotopes are the heavy Te-128 and Te-130, while iodine is a single isotope, I-127, so tellurium's average mass exceeds iodine's despite the lower atomic number.
